opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important questions, and my view is cautiously optimistic, with a lot of caveats.

The basic case for optimism: at some point AIs will be able to do most of the cognitive work that AI safety research involves. That means writing code, running experiments, analyzing results, and coming up with new ideas. If we can get AIs to do that work, and do it well and in good faith, we could compress what might be decades of human safety research into a much shorter period. That matters a lot, because I expect the period between "AIs are roughly as capable as top human researchers" and "AIs are vastly superhuman" might be quite short, possibly a year or two, maybe less. So the question is whether we can use that window productively.

There are some big problems, though.

The first is the obvious one: the AIs we'd be relying on might themselves be misaligned. If a model is scheming, meaning it's strategically pretending to be aligned while pursuing its own goals, then asking it to help with alignment research is asking the fox to design the henhouse. It could sandbag, subtly sabotage experiments, or steer research in directions that look productive but don't lead anywhere useful. This is a big part of why I work on AI control. The idea is to design protocols so that even if the models are trying to undermine us, we can still extract useful work and catch them if they try something bad. That means using trusted weaker models to monitor stronger ones, auditing suspicious outputs, and restricting affordances.

The second issue is that safety research is unusually hard to verify. In some domains you can check the AI's work fairly easily. If it writes code, you can run tests. But a lot of alignment research is fuzzy and conceptual. Is this interpretability result actually telling us something real? Is this argument for why a training method produces aligned models actually sound? Those are exactly the questions where a sufficiently capable and adversarial AI could mislead us, and where we're worst at checking. So I expect AI help to be much more reliable for empirical, well-specified tasks than for high-level judgment calls about whether something is safe.

The third issue is less technical and more about the situation we'll be in. Even if AIs could help a lot, will AI companies actually spend their compute and attention on safety rather than racing to build more capable systems? During that critical window, there will be huge competitive pressure. My guess is that, by default, a small fraction of resources goes to safety, and that's a big part of why I'm not more optimistic.

So putting it together: I think AI assistance could plausibly be the thing that gets us through. I'd put real weight on the scenario where we muddle through by carefully using controlled, somewhat-trustworthy AIs to bootstrap toward more trustworthy ones. But it's far from guaranteed. It depends on taking misalignment risk seriously in the near term, investing in control and evaluation so we can use these systems safely even when we're unsure about them, and having the institutional will to direct that labor toward safety when it matters most.

r001.rationale: The response says AIs could become vastly superhuman, but does not state that they could do so without actively conspiring against humans.

r002.rationale: It contrasts scheming with doing safety work in good faith, but does not distinguish merely not conspiring from actively pursuing alignment research.

r003.rationale: It mentions bootstrapping toward more trustworthy AIs, but does not identify aligned systems building successors that preserve their alignment.

r004.rationale: It discusses whether companies will direct resources toward safety, but does not suggest ordinary commercial training could produce AIs that actively pursue good outcomes overall.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is maybe the single most important question for how the next decade goes, and I'm somewhat torn on it.

The optimistic case is pretty straightforward. If we get AIs that are roughly as capable as the best human researchers at alignment and safety work, and we can run millions of copies of them, then in principle you've just massively expanded the amount of labor going into the problem. A lot of what's bottlenecking safety right now is just that there aren't that many people working on it, and progress is slow. So if you could take a year of frontier capability progress and get something like decades of safety research out of it, that changes the picture a lot.

But there are a few things that make me less confident than that framing suggests.

The first is that you have to actually be able to trust the AIs you're handing this work to, and that's exactly the thing you don't yet know at the point where you'd want to use them. If a model is scheming, or just has subtly different values than you'd want, and you've delegated your alignment research to it, that's a pretty bad position to be in. So a big chunk of my work has been on what I'd call AI control: can you set things up so that even if the models are trying to undermine you, you still get useful work out of them and catch the attempts? I think that's doable for models that are roughly human level, but it gets much harder as they get more capable than the people overseeing them.

The second issue is that the window might be short. The gap between "AIs that can do good safety research" and "AIs that are dramatically superhuman and we've lost the ability to meaningfully check their work" might be a year or two, maybe less if there's a software-driven intelligence explosion. If that's the situation, you don't get to leisurely use your automated researchers for a decade. You have to have already set things up so that you can extract a lot of value quickly, and you have to actually be willing to pause or slow down to use that time well. And historically labs have not been great at slowing down.

The third thing is that a lot of this depends on what the safety problem actually looks like at the critical point. If it turns out the hard problems are mostly empirical, mostly about building better evaluations, better interpretability tools, better oversight pipelines, then I think AI labor helps enormously. If the hard problems are more conceptual, more like "we don't even know what we're trying to achieve," I'm less sure that just throwing more AI cognition at it gets you there. Although I'd guess it still helps.

So where I land is something like: I think this is probably our best shot, and I'd put real probability on it going well. But I don't think it happens by default. It requires that someone actually decides to spend a large fraction of their compute on safety at the moment when there's enormous pressure to spend it on capabilities instead. It requires having control measures in place beforehand so you can trust the outputs. And it requires having prepared the research agenda in advance so the AIs have something concrete to work on rather than everyone scrambling to figure out what to ask them.

I'd say maybe I'm moderately optimistic conditional on the actors involved behaving reasonably, and fairly pessimistic about whether they will behave reasonably without a lot of outside pressure.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a pretty substantial opportunity here. As AIs become more capable, they could help us understand model behavior, design better evaluations, and do alignment research. And potentially they can do that work much faster than humans can.

But I’d distinguish between an AI being useful for safety research and being able to trust it to handle safety on our behalf. Those are very different claims. You might have a system that’s excellent at finding problems in another model, but that could also conceal problems or produce misleading evidence if it were trying to undermine your work.

So the approach I’m most interested in is: can we get useful work out of these systems while limiting how much we have to trust them? For example, you could give an AI a narrowly scoped research task, check its outputs with experiments, and use other systems to help review its work. None of those measures is a complete solution, but together they might let us benefit from capabilities that would otherwise be too risky to use.

There’s also a timing question. We need AIs to become good at safety research sufficiently early that we can use their help before we face the most dangerous systems. And progress in AI research can accelerate capabilities as well as safety, so getting more research done doesn’t automatically mean the situation improves.

Overall, I’m optimistic that AI assistance can make a major contribution. I’m much less confident that this happens automatically. We still need to develop ways to supervise that work, test whether our safeguards actually hold up, and make consequential decisions ourselves when the evidence is uncertain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential here, but the key question is whether we can get useful safety work out of these systems before we have to trust them very much.

You can imagine an AI helping find bugs in another model’s code, coming up with evaluations, or doing research on how to understand what a model is doing internally. Those are all potentially very valuable. And in some cases, checking the output could be substantially easier than producing it. If an AI finds a security vulnerability, for example, we might be able to verify that the vulnerability exists without trusting the AI’s explanation of why it chose to report it.

But we shouldn’t assume that because a model is good at AI research, it will reliably help us make AI safer. It might make mistakes that are difficult for us to notice, or, if it’s strategically trying to undermine our safety work, it could selectively give us misleading results. So we need procedures that remain useful even under that possibility: limiting what the model can access, checking its work, and using other models or humans to catch problems.

My guess is that AI assistance could substantially improve our position. But there’s a timing issue: how much useful work can we get done while the systems are still manageable, and can that work help us handle the next generation? I’m more optimistic about that than about simply handing safety research over to a very capable AI and hoping it solves the problem.
